词汇默写本

上海高中英语 · 沪教版 2022
必修 1–3 ｜ 选择性必修 1–4
1560 个词条 ｜ 1440 个不重复单词 ｜ 28 个单元 ｜ 7 篇故事
5 个勾 = 5 次间隔复习：D0 · D+1 · D+3 · D+7 · D+15

怎么用这本默写本

1. 一行一个词，中间 5 个方框

左边是英文 + 词性，最右边是中文 + 词性，中间 5 个方框。盖住右边做英译中，盖住左边做中译英；两个方向都默对，才在当天的格子里打勾。

2. 5 个勾不是"打 5 次"，而是 5 个复习节点

页眉的 D0 · D+1 · D+3 · D+7 · D+15 就是五个节点：学完当天、次日、第 3 天、第 7 天、第 15 天。哪一次没过，这个词回到 D0 重来。5 个勾全部打满，才算"完全背出"。

3. 先读故事，再默词表

每册词表前面有一篇英文故事，把本册约 200 个目标词串成一个完整故事，目标词加粗。先读故事猜词义，再翻到后面的词表逐词核对，比直接背词表轻松。

4. 遮挡条

最后一页有两条可剪下来的遮挡条：一条盖住中文，一条盖住英文；也可以直接用一张卡片横着挡。

符号含义
D0–D+15五个复习节点，每格打勾代表该次双向默写通过
词性n. 名词 / v. 动词 / adj. 形容词 / adv. 副词 / prep. 介词 / conj. 连词 / num. 数词 / phr. 短语
斜体小字（如 3.1）该词首次出现的册.单元，如 3.1 = 必修三 Unit 1

必修一 · 边读边背

The Lantern in the Dorm

转学生米拉在寄宿学校的第一周：从一只旧灯笼开始，她慢慢读懂新学校的节奏、规则与温度。

Chapter 1 · A Typical Day, Minus the Ordinary

On her first night in the dorm, Mira lay awake until midnight. The digital clock on her desk flashed 00:00, and a small lantern her grandmother had given her glowed on the shelf. It was a unique object in a room full of standard furniture, and it reminded her of home.

It was a typical morning: she stepped onto the bus, thinking about two related questions. Her routine at the new school was still a mystery. The schedule on her phone listed a conference with her senior mentor at nine, a junior class meeting at ten, and a volunteer event in the afternoon. The school was a large organization with a quality reputation, and every aspect of its behaviour code seemed designed to inspire respect.

"Your only goal this week," her partner Theo said at breakfast, "is to acquire one good habit." Theo had a particular attitude toward tradition: he reflected on it, questioned it, but never dismissed it.

Mira selected a type of tea from the machine, pressed the button, and watched the water deliver itself into her cup. Currently, the school was trying to improve its electricity use, so the machine switched off after each cup. A small tip printed on the material beside it explained why.

At the conference, the mentor asked each student to respond to one question: what do you want to earn here? Mira wrote: a description of myself that I can trust. The mentor smiled. "That is a fine challenge," she said. "And a fine element of any exploration."

After class, Mira helped edit the notice board for the volunteer event. The location was the old gym, and the length of the walk there surprised her. On the way she passed a scene she would remember: two senior students teaching a junior one to fold paper lanterns, their hands moving with the ease of long practice.

That night, the death of the clock's battery left the room dark, and Mira laughed. She had come here for freedom, and here it was: a small room, a dead clock, a living lantern, and a routine she was beginning to improve, one ordinary day at a time.

Chapter 2 · A Million Stones, One View

On Saturday the whole class set off for a historic site outside the city. The destination was a former royal court, originally built as a defence against invaders. Nowadays it is a museum, and more than a million visitors walk through its entrance every year.

"It looks amazing in photos," said Theo, "but the structure is what interests me." He pointed at the sculpture in the courtyard: a statue of a general holding a weapon that had never been used in a real battle. "That is not a feature of war," he said. "It is a memory of fear."

Mira opened her blog and began to chat about the view. From the top of the wall, the desert stretched nowhere in particular, and the crowded streets of downtown seemed far away. For a moment she felt embarrassed by her own opinion — that old stones could be energetic — but she wrote it down anyway.

Their guide, a former teacher, explained the origin of the poetry carved on the wall. "These lines were the basis of a whole scientific tradition," she said. "They contribute to our understanding of the stars." Mira began to admire the care behind each line; she could indicate exactly where the stone had been repaired, and she voted to spend the rest of the trip there.

In the afternoon, the class was given an opportunity to settle a small dispute about transport. Some students wanted to walk; others preferred the bus. "Let us put it in an envelope and decide later," said the guide, laughing. Afterwards, they all agreed that the walk had been the real adventure. Mira did not fancy another long walk, but she was glad she had come.

Back at school, Mira tried to position her photos on the blog, but the page kept moving. She was shocked at how much she had written — and altogether happy with it. The trip had disappointed no one.

Chapter 3 · The Label on the Fridge

The next challenge was the convenience store by the facility gate. Mira had never read a food label before; she simply grabbed a snack and threw the packaging away. Then a teenager in her class, Lena, asked her a question that changed her routine: "Do you know where the plastic container goes?"

Lena was a consumer with strong opinions. She had done a project on the global food system, and she could prove that a single amount of wasted food released a surprising amount of greenhouse gas. "Every choice has an impact," she said. "Moreover, the details matter."

They stood in front of the fridge, where frozen food sat beside yoghurt and pudding. "A slim figure on the image is not a health plan," Lena went on. "Actually, most diet advice for teenagers comes from people who want to sell something." She pointed to the source of a claim on a poster and asked Mira to comment on it.

Mira began to tend to agree. She did not want to assume anything without evidence, and she wanted to establish a few rules for herself. Could the school legally permit students to bring their own container? Could the store recycle more and install an energy-efficient fridge? The manager, a retired teacher, listened carefully and did not stress the rules; instead he offered a link to the city's recycling guide.

"Despite the loss of a few customers," he said, "we can do better. We can determine what sells and what is wasted, and we can make the cattle and the groceries part of one honest system." He asked Mira to remind him of the meeting and to apologize to no one for asking.

At lunch, the class held a debate. Mira had to host one table, and she had to keep the discussion equal — every voice, including the quietest junior, should count. She did not fancy public speaking, but she proved to herself that she could do it. By the end, the expert from the city office said the students had made a real impact. The decoration on the wall — a painted label saying "Choose well" — suddenly looked less like decoration and more like advice.

Chapter 4 · A Room with a Soul

Mira's apartment at home had been small, but her dorm room was smaller. On the first occasion she had time to arrange it, she stood on a chair and looked at the ceiling, then at the narrow bed, the curtain, and the poster she had intended to put up. The room was extremely plain, and she preferred it that way — for now.

Her goal was a labour-saving room. She bought a small device that could download her files and software updates, and a lamp that switched itself off. Unfortunately, the company that made the lamp had gone out of business, and the brochure promised more than the lamp could do. She did not argue with it, and she did not want to suffer in silence; she simply grabbed a screwdriver and fixed the switch.

The experiment of living alone was harder than she had expected. She had to boil water for tea, load the washing machine, and regularly check that the petrol heater was off. A percentage of her data disappeared when the Wi-Fi dropped, and a bomb of homesickness hit her on the second night. "You are capable of more than you think," her mother said on the phone. "Definitely."

Her senior friend Theo had a talent for turning a room into a time-honoured place. He brought a small piano downstairs — with the goods lift, since the stairs were too narrow — and played while Mira gathered her stuff. "Music is a technique for surviveing," he said. "It decreases the noise in your head."

On the wall, Mira put a photo of her grandmother's house, an upper-class home from the 1940s with a style all its own. "Every adult I know wants a bigger room," she said. "I want a room with a soul." She recommended the same aim to her partner: choose one thing that will last, and let the rest disappear. Immediately after she said it, the lamp flickered, and they both laughed. Slightly embarrassed, she loaded the photo file again and set it as her screen. The room, at last, had a style of its own — and a responsibility to match.

必修二 · 边读边背

The Risk Report

萨姆和艾达做一份关于“冒险”的课题报告：从安全带、滑雪到冲浪事故，他们逐渐明白风险、判断与成就的关系。

Chapter 1 · Blame the Brain?

Sam had always been a careful boy, the kind who fastens his seat belt before the engine starts and reads every section of the safety card. So when his teacher announced the theme of the term — "No limits" — he felt a familiar pressure in his chest.

"You need a strategy," said Ada, his partner on the project. "Pick one issue, one factor that changes how people take risks, and study it properly." Ada was independent and ambitious; she had already written to a charity that studied a rare disease of the nervous system. Her confidence did not impress Sam. It frightened him a little, and a frightening idea followed: what if she was right?

Their first interview was with a former adventurer named Ruth, who had once tried to ski across a continent and had the boot to prove it. "People blame the brain for every bad judgement," Ruth said. "But a chemical signal is not a solution. It is only a factor." She showed them a statistic: most accidents happen to people who believe they are reliable judges of their own limit.

Sam began to conduct his own attempt to measure risk. He built a small vehicle with a limited range and a sensor that could contain a reaction time test. The results were incredible: students who said they were responsible were not always the fastest to adapt. "To what extent," Ada asked, "does curiosity change the account?"

The answer came from an eyewitness at the base of the mountain: a native guide who had watched a surfing accident from the shore. She could reveal exactly what went wrong, and she did not blame the young man. "He was dizzy from the cold," she said. "Preserve the story, not the shame."

The author of their report turned out to be Sam himself. He wrote the final section in one sitting, and for the first time he felt that his achievement was not a limit he had avoided, but one he had chosen. "I want to quit being afraid of fear," he told Ada. She smiled. "That is an issue worth a whole series."

Chapter 2 · One Episode at a Time

The school launched an experiment: every class would produce one episode of a podcast series about learning. Sam and Ada were given the previous year's recordings and a brief from the head teacher: keep it positive, keep it brief, and quote real students.

Their first job was to document the school's resources. The library had a lecture room, a recording studio, and a supply of old microphones. "We are eager to help," said the librarian, who frequently updated the notice board. "Otherwise," she added, "nobody knows what we have."

The theme of their episode was motivate — how to keep a good mood when exams approach. They interviewed a devoted teacher who used creative tasks and a performance night to to give students a sense of satisfaction. "A positive effect on concentration is obviously worth the effort," she said. "But you must recognize that cooperation takes practice, and that mental health is not a debate."

Then a hurricane hit the county. It tore a path through the valley, and the school became a centre for aid. Students donated clothes and food; the supply of water was tight for two days. "We need a procedure," Ada said, "and we need everyone to be aware of it." The head teacher asked Sam to summarize the plan, to propose a rota for the volunteers, and to promote it on the school Wi-Fi page. A charity for cancer research sent a thank-you card.

That week, a major accident on the coast road made the news: a small boat had tried to sail into the ocean and had lost its signal. The audience for their podcast grew. "Indeed, we are addicted to our phones," one student said on air, "but the benefit of a real conversation is that it can prevent a bad decision."

The episode ended with a quote from the master of the school: "Academic success is not a cure for loneliness, and a uniform is not an identity." The class clapped. Sam felt the function of the project change: it was no longer about grades. "Let us pursue this," he said. "Series two starts next week."

Chapter 3 · A Letter That Travelled

For the third episode, the team turned to a bigger range of questions. A billion people, the figure went, would be affected by a climate that was changing at an alarming rate. "Can we predict the next chain reaction?" Ada asked.

Their science teacher was concerned but calm. "Agriculture and hunting both threaten species with extinction," she said. "Somehow, the youth of today must admit that unfamiliar facts are not the enemy." She asked them to measure what they could and to imply nothing they had not tested.

Sam wrote a formal letter to a major official at the city's environment office, asking for an interview. To his surprise, the answer came by exchange of emails: a fluent young officer invited them to a range of meetings. "Madam," Sam began, then stopped. "Therefore," he wrote instead, "we would be grateful if you could advertise our advertisement — sorry, our campaign — to your contact list."

The officer laughed when she read it. "Absolutely no problem," she said. "But let me contrast two options: a fund for local design projects, or a balance between available resources. Which do you desire?" The team chose the second, and promised to reduce waste plus report every process honestly.

That spring, a graduate student showed them how to test a cloth net against mud and string in a mirror of the local river. "We must tear down the old figure of the youth who does not care," she said. "Eventually, the concerned will fund the work." A flight over the delta showed the official how much had changed significantly in a decade.

Sam wrote back faithfully — a word Ada teased him for — and signed the letter formally. In the final episode of the series, the range of voices was wider than ever: a farmer, a student, an officer, a scientist. "We are not concerned about blame any more," Sam said. "We are concerned about the next measure."

Chapter 4 · The Old Man and the Net

The last chapter took Sam to a fishing village his grandfather had left a decade ago. The atmosphere was salt and rope and grain dust. An old fisherman named Elias agreed to take him out, on one request: no camera, no title, just work.

"You want to gain a story," Elias said. "Then maintain the line and do not attack the sea." He showed Sam how to wrap the rope around a brick to keep the net steady, how to approach a shark without bleeding, and how to read a sharp change in the sky by the colour of the water.

They set out before dawn. The boat was small but self-sufficient, with a professional target: enough fish for the village, no more. "Curious animals are not a threat," Elias said. "Intelligent ones are." A bite on the line, a struggle on the deck, and then a shark that attacked the catch and destroyed the net. Sam felt the boat sink slightly and his confidence with it. The smell of the catch would attract gulls for hours.

"A setback," Elias said, "is not a failure. Realistic men lack nothing but luck." He took a clue from the wind and changed course. By noon they had outstanding strength in their arms and a shortage of nothing. The village institute later gave Elias a medal for fifty years at sea.

Sam wrote the final script that night. The title was simple: *The Old Man and the Net*. His teacher said the ending was false — too happy. Sam defeated the doubt by adding a line: "Ahead of us the weather changed dramatically, and we turned back." He chose to leave the literature of the sea unfinished, and he permanently kept the brick on his desk as a paperweight, a clue to what he had learned. Skin and bone, he wrote, are what a story is made of.

必修三 · 边读边背

The Fourth Estate Club

妮娅加入校报记者团，从一张照片、一次采访到一期特刊，逐渐理解“媒体”两个字的重量。

Chapter 1 · The Annual Issue

Nia had never written for a journal before, so when the school's media committee announced that the annual special issue needed a photographer, she signed up joyfully. The editor, Kai, was a rare character: calm under pressure, flexible with deadlines, and entirely without emotion when correcting an error.

"Every entry must illustrate one idea," Kai said. "We publish throughout the region, so ensure that nothing affects the overall tone." He gave her a collection of old issues, each with an entertaining column: a novel review, a plot summary of a super soundtrack, an interview with an astronaut about a system crash, and a report on a disaster in a province where a flour factory had burned.

The journalist in charge of the subway story had average soccer knowledge but a horrible sense of direction. "I spot the custom of the ordinary female fan," she said, "and then I perceive the emotion behind the click." Her outline was broad but authority on the subject was clear.

Nia needed permission to photograph a civilization exhibition, and the nationality of each character on display had to be confirmed before release. She breathed slowly, merrily humming to keep her calm, and set to work. Innovation, she decided, was not a pack of new gadgets but a way of seeing.

That night the paper went to press. A medical team arrived to treat a visitor who had fainted; the committee confirmed the entry was accurate. "Overall," Kai said, "we have one rare error: the astronaut's nationality is wrong in column three." Nia laughed, joyfully again. "At least the photographer got the emotion right," she said.

Chapter 2 · The Journey of a T-shirt

The second story began with a guy in a gym who sweated through his jeans and asked, "Where does a T-shirt come from?" Nia followed the trail: cotton fields, a harvest of honey-coloured liquid, a flood that ruined half the crop, and a port where dozens of containers waited to be exported.

"Every quantity has a price," said a worker at the treatment plant. "Iron, wine, smog, insect—everything involves profit and income." He showed her how to calculate the economic cost of a single application of dye. "Accurate figures are remarkable," he said, "because most people hesitate to ask."

At the discount store, Nia watched a majority of shoppers protest about the bitter flavour of a new roast while others slide past awkwardly. A bar of soap, a kit for repairs, a breath of fresh air in the smog—the shop was a habitat for small decisions. "We import the equipment, we replace the labels, and we certify nothing," the owner admitted. "Cash is advanced, and the operation continues."

The mission was to rescue the truth from the marketing. Nia tracked an overseas version of the same shirt and found a living wage missing from the slide show. "The economic benefit is specific," her editor said, "but so is the harm." She wrote the final chapter by hand, and the movement of her pen felt like a small protest of its own.

Chapter 3 · The Faces We Choose

The third issue was about faces. On campus, Nia put a sample of photos on a display board and asked students to react. The pattern was odd: almost everyone chose the same ideal profile, a delicate representation that no individual actually matched.

"Make-up is a practical art," said one girl, elegant in a metal-framed mirror. "But the trend stretches a normal face into a shallow symbol." A broad survey enabled Nia to observe how gender and occupation vary the context of beauty. "Sex sells, but personality exists too," a boy said, and the emphasis shifted.

The external impression of a generation is constantly under construction. "We ignore the effort behind a shave or a suit," said a photographer, "and we dive into hide-and-seek with our own image." Her duty, she said, was to carve a space where a wedding photo and a jogging photo could sit side by side. "Various branches of one family," she called them.

There was relief in the mass of replies, and a different sort of answer: further down the column, a specific concept appeared again and again — beauty is a symbol we choose, not a rule we follow. The surrounding noise of make-up ads faded. Nia wrote the highlight of the issue: "Nothing about a face is short-sighted; only the way we look at it is."

Chapter 4 · A Tale from the South

The final issue took Nia further than the campus. She won a scholarship to join a conservation foundation in Australia for a month — a tough competition, and a specific qualification in photography helped.

The flight engine hummed. She read the guideline for visitors and tried to construct a diagram of the trip. "Seek the romantic highlight, not the extra souvenir," Kai had said. "And declare nothing you cannot prove."

At the foundation, she met a charitable ranger who had spent a decade employing students to track kangaroos. "Recreation and conservation can compete," he said, "but sufficient enthusiasm persuades people to engage." He employed a specific concept: the agricultural drought had harmed the habitat, and a mosquito plague followed.

She went jogging before dawn, then they drove the highway and saw a deer-like dinosaur of a machine, a plate of solar panels, and a nearby studio where an opera was being postponed because of the heat. "Anxious tourists get scared," the ranger calmly said, "but a dolphin and a whale do not care about our schedule." Nia revised her chapter that night: the tale would be about movement, not escape.

On the last day she watched a flash of lightning over the water and felt the foundation of her own confidence settle. The recreation of a concept she had once thought romantic — the wild — now had a guideline and a qualification attached. Further effort, she wrote, is the only convincing chapter.

选必一 · 边读边背

The Chocolate Theory

艾薇的姑妈开巧克力店，她一边做“幸福”课题，一边在岛屿、网红与味觉之间寻找答案。

Chapter 1 · A Theory of Small Pleasures

Ivy's aunt runs a chocolate shop in a suburb of the city. Every item in the drawer behind the counter has a story, and Ivy had heard them all. "People associate chocolate with happiness," her aunt said, "but that is a theory, not a fact."

Ivy was writing a presentation on happiness for her nutrition class. Her tablet was full of scientific evidence, yet the overall picture was miserable: a decade of studies, a million opinions. "Lack of sleep affects mood," she read. "Anxiety and depression are not a fashion." The chemical release in the brain that chocolate promotes is real, but the tone of the ads imply that a portion can cure cancer.

"You consume a calorie and afterwards feel disappointed," her aunt said. "That is the phenomenon." She had a solid recipe for a composition of flavours, and she was committed to it. "Self-reliance and discipline," she said, "persuade people better than a golf tournament ever could."

At school, the class had to wrestle with a question: can mutual cooperation and commitment survive a greedy market? A journalist came to speak. "Mostly, the industry adopts a fry-everything approach," she said. "In contrast, small shops sacrifice profit for quality." Her urge was for students to appreciate essential, vital, crucial things: sleep, cycle rides, a poet's line, a friend's tone of voice.

"Optimistic?" the teacher asked. "Incredibly," Ivy said. She had evidence: a consumption study her aunt had cooperated on suggested that a mutual commitment to small pleasures could release the pressure of a depressed mood. "Abandon the fashion of the big cure," she wrote. "Keep the small essential." The class clapped, and her aunt sent a box of tablet-shaped chocolates to celebrate.

Chapter 2 · The Island That Kept Giving

That summer Ivy joined a conservation camp on a distant island. The tide came in fast, the waves broke over the shelter, and the mosquitoes were widespread. "Nevertheless," the camp leader said, "we preserve what we can."

The island's rural landscape was a plain of native grass and antique walls. A fellow volunteer named Jun, who had been nominated for a youth award, showed her a visual map of the habitat. "We cannot predict the overflow of the tide," he said, "but we can defend the structure of the dormitory."

A victim of the last flood became an advocate for the ban. Anger and frustration rose when a campaign to ban garbage near the pub was skipped by the council. "Inform the folk," Jun said. "Access to clean water is a responsibility, not a favour." Ivy wrote an essay with a precise perspective: the urban visitors brought varied habits, and a widespread intention was not enough. She became convinced that the opposing side had a point about violence in the contest for land.

The appointment with the dentist had to wait; the barbecue and the recycle bin took priority. An energy-efficient lamp was installed in the dormitory, and a tune from a bride's wedding drifted over the water. "Bless this place," the bridegroom said, and even the ancestors seemed to listen.

Their marathon needed a sponsor. Ivy wrote to a charitable foundation; the reply asked them to conserve, to recycle, and to involve the native folk in every decision. "Enthusiasm is rewarding," the letter said, "but a campaign must transform habits, not just stretch them." The calligraphy on the old pub sign — a structure of precise strokes — seemed to threaten to fall. They restored it forever with a tune from the island and a ban on plastic.

By August, Ivy's perspective had changed: the island was not a shelter from the city but a laboratory of responsibility. "We cannot preserve everything," she wrote in her final essay. "But we can defend what we love."

Chapter 3 · The Price of a Trend

In autumn, a celebrity came to the canteen to launch a drink. The advertisement said the ingredient was genuine and the toast on the bottle was harmonious with nature. Ivy, now writing for a monthly publication, was asked to cover it.

"I smell a trick," said her editor. "Anyhow, check the contract." The agency had hired a psychologist and a borderline artist, respectively responsible for the mood and the look, to stimulate desire, and a specialist to guarantee the harvest of a crop that did not exist. The finding was identical to a case Ivy had read about: fake reviews, a discount that was contrary to the true price, and a trendsetter paid to display a luxury lifestyle.

"Identify the origin," her editor said. "That is the priority." Ivy went to a cottage in the countryside where cotton grocery bags were packed by hand. An academic quote on the wall said: "Commercialize nothing you cannot wrap in truth." The ethical principle was conventional but unusual in practice.

She spotted the faulty sample in the display and complained to the madam at the desk. "Madam," she said, "your weekly advertisement is false, and the lunar festival jewellery is not available." The manager asked her to adjust the loose pack in her suitcase and to faithfully report what she saw. "We will hire an agency to investigate," he said. "But we will not advertise a purchase we cannot guarantee."

The story ran under the headline "Billion-dollar Trend". Ivy had rescued the concept of ideal from the abstract and given it a concrete sample: a cotton bag, a crop of honest work, and a contract worth reading.

Chapter 4 · A Pinch of Salt

The last chapter began with a bath of steam and a pinch of salt. Ivy had signed up for an elective on taste, and the class was meeting in a tent on the roof. "Perceive before you judge," said the teacher, handing out raw cabbage, onion, and a ripe peach.

The peach was exceptionally sweet, and the raw cabbage was unpleasant at first. Ivy's tongue could detect bitter, salty, sour, and spicy easily, but she could not distinguish two creamy desserts. "You are somewhat sensitive to texture," the teacher said, "but your appetite is ruled by scent." The claim was a riddle; the combination of flavour and memory differs from person to person.

That weekend, the class went on a hike. A warning on the lamp post said the thunderstorm would expand. They constructed a facility of ropes and barriers, and a creature — merciless in the dark — stared from the trees. "Do not panic," said the teacher. "React slowly." A whisper of wind, a flow of quantity rain, and then an incident: a student buryed his ankle in a hole and barked in pain.

The injury was not serious. "Grateful for the warning," the student said. "I will investigate my preference for short cuts." The principle was simple: a complaint is a challenge, not a barrier. Ivy's ringtone disturbed the silence, and she switched it off, bothered by her own noise.

Back home, she wrote the final chapter of her project: impairment of one sense can sharpen another, and a rescue can begin with a pinch of salt. "The frequency of radiation from a phone is not the point," she wrote. "The encounter with a creature in a thunderstorm is." Her aunt read it and insisted on one more dessert.

加粗词为本册词表目标词；先读故事猜词义，再翻到后面的词表逐词核对与默写。

选必二 · 边读边背

The Letter in the Mailbox

欧文在一间小办公室做职员，一封奖学金申请信把他带回祖父的民权往事，也带回自己的职业选择。

Chapter 1 · Worthwhile Work

Owen found his vocation by accident. He was a clerk in a mailbox-sized office, scanning letters for a counsellor who had minimum patience and a sensational catalogue of qualifications. One rough morning a candidate enclosed a certificate and a passionate note: "I want to gain a scholarship to study drama."

"Sincerely," the note ended, "approve me or cease." Owen was amused. He tossed the letter on the edge of the desk and went to wander by the canal, where a bare-foot child recited a column of occupations: assistant, clerk, tailor, servant. "Suitable work deserves respect," the child said, and Owen felt the shaft of an idea descend.

He began to loosen his circumstances. A goat on the territory of the church sowed seeds of entertainment for the whole town; a rocket of proof arrived from a patent office; an inquiry about freedom and the constitution landed in his mailbox. "Exaggeration is a threat to reform," his grandfather said. "Illegal arrest and prison are not proof of justice."

His grandfather had been arrested in the decline of the old racial order, humiliated for a damage he had not caused, and discriminated against by circumstance alone. The discrimination was written into the law. "Mission," he said, "is to impress the insight on the next generation." Owen wrote it all down, enthusiastic at last. The column he published, "Worthwhile Work", began with the child's line and ended with his grandfather's threat to reform: "Freedom is not a scholarship; it is a citizen's capacity to approve his own life."

That night he scanned the letter again. The candidate's drama was nonsense to the minimum-wage clerk, but it was sensational to the counsellor. Owen tossed it back — and then, for freedom's sake, enclosed his own certificate.

Chapter 2 · The Device That Knew Too Much

The second chapter belonged to a device Owen did not trust. His employer had bought a digital assistant with an outgoing profile and an adorable voice. "It will analyse your status and clarify your priorities," the employer said. "Consequently, you will work faster."

The device could log every instant of his day. It could scan a handkerchief and tell him it was dirty; it could weigh a kettle and pause the boil. "Rarely does a machine dare to compromise," Owen said. "It is consistently neutral."

Then a nasty message appeared on a social profile: an old photo, a fleeting joke, a dozen gossip items. "Untag me," Owen prayed, but the exposure had already done its harm. His potential employer called. "We need an objective version of this emergency," she said. "Instantly."

Owen had no choice but to withdraw the post; he deleted the account and confronted the mechanical rhyme of the algorithm. "Inaccurate data can damage a reputation," he said. "Devices should be compatible with dignity, not just with mechanical speed."

He would bet that the watch on his wrist and the belt at his waist were logging him too. His sympathetic friend Ada (a genius with wire and plug) helped him reverse the version of the story. They comprised a component list: the clue, the constant dare, the instant pause. "Confront the foggy mist," she said. "Clarify the canal, not the globe."

At the estate office, a desperate merchant with a hip injury and a lung problem asked for help. Owen absorbed the intense details — the weed by the pond, the wire across the canal, the blank expression on the assistant's face — and classified them objectively. "Consequently," he wrote, "the harm was fleeting, the compromise constant." The situation was mechanical, but the person was not; the story made his sister weep.

He published the version under a neutral title. "Prior to the device," he wrote, "we had sympathy. Subsequent to it, we have data. The former is harder to analyse, and worth more."

Chapter 3 · A Triangle of Beauty

The third chapter was about art. Owen's professor had a vision of a city where beauty was not a luxury but a property of every street. "Gradually," she said, "a sculptor can change a triangle of concrete into a splendid public room."

They visited a controversial exhibition of cubism. A brilliant young genius — a scream of colour against a jungle of grey — had used leather, steel, and a ruined opera poster to compose a symphony of shapes. The criticism was substantial: some said the work denied emotion; others applauded its evaluative practical security and its straightforward interpretation of inner life. "Superb," the professor said. "Remarkable output for a tailor's servant." The artist was, in fact, a tailor's son, and the royal family had once favoured his distinctive adaptation of noble fantasy.

Then a robber broke into the gallery. The absence of a guard was a grave financial mistake; a funeral of reputation followed for the security company. "Deny nothing," said the professor. "Evaluate the division of labour, not the characteristic of a category."

Owen wrote about the anniversary of the gallery's founding and the emphasis on maturity in its curation. The striking thing was how complicated the interpretation had become: a controversial painting could compete with a symphony for attention, and a simple triangle could convey a sense of security.

"Compose your own visual essay," the professor told him. "Output is not quantity; it is devotion." Owen gradually understood. The finance of art was complicated, but the emotion was straightforward: a splendid room, a brilliant line, a remarkable absence of fear.

Chapter 4 · The Leaf That Stayed

The last chapter began with a blank wall and a ladder. Owen's grandfather, a humble lawyer, had spent his liberty defending a navy crew and a communist amateur painter. "Initially," he said, "I had a pessimistic belief that the law was a sin. Then I met a man who could negotiate with dignity."

The painter lived in a humble room with a carpet, a blanket, and a pond of light on the floor. He was severely ill and confined to bed, and he had a fate-like belief that he would die when the last leaf fell. "Nonsense," said his neighbour, an amateur herb-grower. "But fascinating nonsense."

The old man assigned himself a mission: to paint a leaf that would never fall. He climbed a ladder amid the shade of the brick wall, bow and arrow of his brush in hand, and dedicated the night to it. Subsequent to that night, the outstanding leaf stayed firm on its stem, and the painter, acknowledgeing the hint, began to pursue life again.

"Ambitious?" the lawyer asked. "No," the neighbour said. "Principled." The transformation was extraordinary, a lesson in persistence: a sorrow became a stability, a steel of the inner kind. The expense was a severe cold, and the involvement of the whole street; the welfare of one man became a corresponding labour of many.

Owen interacted with the story as an adaptation: he classifyed it as romantic, but the manner of its telling was straightforward. "Liberation," his grandfather said, "is a capacity to confront a beam of light and a blank wall at once." Succeeding generations, he wrote, should seize the liberty to accompany the weak.

选必三 · 边读边背

The Island Curriculum

玛雅带着相机去一座偏远海岛做课程项目：她学会用当地人的眼光看荒野、时间与语言。

Chapter 1 · The Island Curriculum

Maya's project began with an airline ticket and a deadline. Her curriculum at school required a photographer to document a remote island, where a minority of students studied in an isolated school. "It is relevant to our course," her teacher said. "You will overcome your fear of flying."

The island was awesome: a frozen shoreline, an eagle on a roof, and a giant cave that the residents called sacred. A tribe of hunters had lived there for centuries, and their vocabulary for the sea was richer than any biology textbook. "We rely on the tide," an old woman said. "The wilderness is our curriculum."

Maya had to grasp the local accent and sew a waterproof cover for her camera with a needle and thread from a circus tent. She joined a bowling match in the venue to greet the residents, and a nephew and niece taught her to hop across the rocks. "Inevitably, you will grab the wrong angle," a photographer said. "Scale is a matter of geometry."

The demand for fluency in English was enormous, but the rigid timetable left little room for restricted subjects like art. "Let us restore the atmosphere of a harsh winter," the head teacher said. "Visible thunder is coming; stay relevant, stay resolved."

A trunk of old maps lay beside a coffin-shaped rock; the channel was navigable only at high tide, and memories of an invasion made the elders arise early. On the last morning, Maya subscribed to the island's mail and photographed a lyrics sheet blowing in the wind. The conflict between budget and ambition was inevitably part of the story, but the horizon looked wider than before. "Impressive," her teacher wrote. "You found the angle that most people miss."

Chapter 2 · The Object and the Story

Back in the city, Maya's next assignment was a museum exhibition on colonial trade. The gallery was full of sentimental objects: a mirror from a colonial house, a vase of precious porcelain, and a monument to a soldier who had defeated an invasion. "Every object has a political dimension," the curator said. "We must justify nothing; we must explain."

The theft happened on a frosty morning. A diamond was missing from a temporary case; the receptionist had seen a suspicious applicant slip a folder into a laptop bag. "Do not mask the facts," the curator said. "Submit the initial report and resist the tendency to blame the guards**."

Maya felt annoyed by the friction between the permanent staff and the joint security team. She had to load her camera, pour over the critical details, and ultimately secure the ongoing debate on camera. "In comparison with last year, theft is up," a guard said. "Currency for insurance is short; licences for new cameras are delayed."

A reluctant witness, a woman with a purse and a mask, spoke of a frightening shark tank in the old gallery: "Flu and virus scares closed it once; tobacco smoke ruined the tubes." The museum's reputation was at risk, and a bank loan could not repair the fright of the visitors. Her testimony was, ultimately, a criterion for the debate: who owns a monument?

"Astonishing," Maya wrote in her folder. "Primitive tools, hazardous friction, abnormal load — but the jazz of the ongoing debate is ultimately about possession." She felt guilty for enjoying the story, but the platform was hers: she could compare dimensions and resist easy answers.

Chapter 3 · The Mirror and the Shadow

Maya's next session was with a novelist who wrote about the body. "Beauty is a symbol, not a moral," the novelist said. "Unceasing images confuse us; the root of the crisis is comparison." She had a philosophy of comfort: ease the shadow, do not reject it.

Maya interviewed a student named Ada, whose ambition was to attain a "perfect" proportion. "I undergo a routine of surgical videos every night," Ada said. "Unrealistic? Yes. But the consequence of not trying feels worse." She was embarrassed and upset, and her motivation would swing from hope to nightmare.

"Tackle it at a pace you can bear," the novelist told her. "Boost your patience; engage with a profession that values muscle and mind, not pearly wrinkles." Ada confided that she had undergone a massive shift after a vivid episode in a curtained room: her jaw and cheek hurt, her forehead was hot, and she felt a mighty flame of shame.

The article was critical but kind. "Behave like a friend, not a judge," Maya wrote. "Decrease the volume of noise; refresh the channel." She added a tale from the island: a pure stream, a comfortable silence, a significance beyond makeup. "Alcohol and cigarette ads sell a nightmare," she wrote. "Insurance and tax forms do not."

The abuse of images had a cost, and Maya said so. The session ended with Ada smiling at her own reflection. The episode was not resolved, but the consequence was a new motivation: to tackle the crisis one pace at a time.

Chapter 4 · The Words That Stay

The last chapter of Maya's project was about words. She went to a literature festival where a classic novel was being adapted for the stage. "The plot is complex," the director said, "but its charm is simple: a portrayal of integrity in a tragic era."

Maya's estimate was that the setting — a grand house with a mysterious cage and a fox in the garden — would tempt any perceptive reader. The formation of the story had evolved from a comic sketch into a gripping tale of rebellion. "Universally, readers delight in a revelation," the director said. "A burst of laughter, then a burst of sorrow."

At the interval, a kindergarten teacher told Maya about a cybercrime: someone had hacked a parcel inspection system and exposed private data. "Subjective judgments are dangerous," she said. "We need fibre optics, not artificial intelligence alone." A microscope in the buffet hall became a symbol of the inspection we owe the truth.

The alternative was superior: a delicate knit of Confucianism and modern law, extending moral integrity universally. "Combine the elegant sleeve of tradition with the peak of science," the director said. "Rent a horn, murder a cliché, reject the idiot narrative." Maya laughed, but she wrote it down.

"Civilians are not innocent by default," she wrote. "Soul and vulnerability are the plot." The comedy ended with a grand spectacular; the tragic era was exposed, and the delight was real.

加粗词为本册词表目标词；先读故事猜词义，再翻到后面的词表逐词核对与默写。

选必四 · 边读边背

The Signal and the Story

播客记者艾里斯追一条台风新闻：从抢眼的画面到可靠的证词，她学会分辨“报道”与“理解”。

Chapter 1 · The Signal and the Storm

Iris's podcast began with a tip from a witness. A typhoon had hit the coast, and the coverage on the main channel was all dramatic footage and prejudice: a suspect kidnapped by the flood, a clinic swept away, a lamb dragged from a dock. "Coverage is not comprehension," her editor said. "Examine the testimony; cite a reliable source."

Iris took a highway to the zone alongside a minor official. "The network here is unregulated," he said. "Prosecute the cheats, not the victims." She watched a spontaneous transition: neighbours shaved ice from a bruised arm, lowered a boat under an arch, and captured the rhythm of a contemporary rescue.

She tried to trace the money behind the story. Her instinct told her the story was bigger than the agenda of any outlet. "Reality is compelling enough," she said. "Blame is easy; comprehension is hard." She recorded aboard a rescue boat, the expectation rising as the water fell. "Emerge from the sweep," a rescuer said. "Do not drag the camera into the mud."

The episode, unscripted and spontaneous, won a minor award. "No envy," her editor said. "Outlook matters more than awards." Iris wrote the final line with comprehension: "A socialist zone is not a headline; it is a network of people who emerge together."

Chapter 2 · The Longevity Clinic

The second episode took Iris to a corporation on the frontier of ageing. The entrepreneur behind it had a script: "Immortality is not a mere dream; it is purely a matter of mechanics." A transplant of young tissue, a drill of new drugs, a dynamic career — the pitch posed a severe question: who can afford to sustain it?

The architect of the clinic was bearded and magnificent in a white coat. "We propose a fundamentally new mode," he said. "Not to dismiss death, but to occupy the interval." His clients sighed with hope; his opponents condemned the debt it would create. "Hence the tension," Iris said. "Owe nothing to legend."

A criminal case exploded that week: a sneaky infection in a vulnerable patient, a severe deterioration, a career smashed. "Miraculously, she did not drown or choke," a nurse said. "But the resistance to regulation is urgent to address." The gender of the patient, the mechanics of the glowing machine — none of it fundamentally changed the harmony needed between profit and care.

A doctor threatened to resign; a sneeze in the waiting room was enough to empty it. The silence began to frustrate her. Iris had to bend over her notes, and felt her alertness sink. "Forgive me," the entrepreneur said with a shrug. "Tension sells." "Dynamic tension," she replied, "not debt." She let the recording run, and the script wrote itself.

Chapter 3 · The Ethics of the Table

The food episode began with a frog in a damp stream and a statistic on a chart: numerous species were in collapse. Iris took a ferry across the strait to a butcher's outlet, where a monstrous predator — a breeder's prize pork — hung in the window. "Distressing," the butcher said. "But demand is dominance."

Meanwhile, an association for recreation and diversity was trying to prohibit the cruel confinement of animals in urban basins. "We monitor the stock, label the fare, and extract the truth," a vet said. "The administration must handle the shortage of protein without destruction of the nest."

Iris pretended to be a customer and fetched a teapot from a bakery beside the stream. A bat distracted her; garlic and bacon aroused her appetite. "Apparently, the legal boundary is damp," the baker said. "Install a circuit that automatically monitors the fertilizer and the mineral input."

At the market, a water buffalo floated in the mud while a vendor marvelled at the diversity of ancestral cuisine. "Ritual matters," she said. "Domestically grown stock has a tolerance for hostile weather." A hostile expansion of factory farms, however, had aroused sympathy for the predator and the frog alike.

"Hence the boundary," Iris said. "Sympathy without statistics is merely distressing." She closed the episode with a label on a pork outlet: "Apparently, ethics is what we extract from ritual and evidence — and what we prohibit out of respect."

Chapter 4 · The Next Big Thing

The final episode was about technology. Iris met a consultant who had drawn the outline of a virtual world: a mode of leisure in which an adolescent could invest in a clone of herself and assess the gravity of choices in a concrete phase of life. "It is a vast domain," he said. "But slight errors in the hardware can precede disaster."

A broadcast from the launch site showed a premier astronaut proceeding along a pipe toward the hatch. "Groundbreaking," the anchor said. "A seed of a new orbit." The telescope tracked a bubble of hydrogen; the generator hummed; a cord an inch from the fuel line was checked twice.

"Infer from the directory," the consultant said. "Demonstrate the expertise, not just the hardware." Iris interviewed an adolescent gamer who had upgraded her virtual avatar. "Inappropriate content is a breast of the same problem," the girl said. "Recognition is not the same as accomplishment."

The drug of speed, the acid of envy, the premature launch — the story had everything. "Assess what can underlie a groundbreaking broadcast," Iris said. "Common sense, concrete tests, and a slight doubt." Volunteers distribute water at the gate; the intervening years had been kind, and for a moment Iris felt faint with relief. The astronaut waved from the hatch, and the universe seemed, for a moment, vast and kind.

加粗词为本册词表目标词；先读故事猜词义，再翻到后面的词表逐词核对与默写。
